meta.name: Certified Kubernetes Security Specialist (CKS)
meta.notes: [bulk-tag pass: added `cks` tag to 61 questions] [cks batch 1: 13 balanced rewrites — recall=0]

questions.question: A namespace `prod` contains a web app that should only accept traffic from Pods within the same namespace. Which NetworkPolicy spec correctly restricts ingress to only Pods inside `prod`?
options: Use `namespaceSelector: {matchLabels: {kubernetes.io/metadata.name: prod}}` in the ingress rule with `podSelector: {}`
Use `ipBlock: {cidr: 0.0.0.0/0}` with except clauses for the namespace CIDR range
Use `podSelector: {matchLabels: {app: web}}` in the ingress rule to restrict by app label
Use an egress rule with `namespaceSelector: {}` to block all outbound traffic from the namespace
questions.explanation: To restrict ingress to only Pods within the same namespace, the NetworkPolicy ingress rule must use `namespaceSelector` matching the namespace's own label (`kubernetes.io/metadata.name: prod`). `podSelector: {}` in the ingress block means all pods from that namespace. `ipBlock` operates at the IP level, not namespace level. Egress rules don't restrict incoming traffic.

questions.question: You run kube-bench against your cluster and it reports: `1.2.6 Ensure that the --authorization-mode argument is not set to AlwaysAllow.` What is the correct remediation?
options: Set `--enable-admission-plugins=NodeRestriction` to restrict which nodes can join the cluster
Set `--authorization-mode=ABAC` with a policy file to replace AlwaysAllow
Set `--authorization-mode=Node,RBAC` on the kube-apiserver and remove AlwaysAllow
Set `--anonymous-auth=false` on the kube-apiserver to reject unauthenticated requests
questions.explanation: The CIS benchmark requires that `AlwaysAllow` is not used as it bypasses all authorization. The correct production mode is `Node,RBAC`: Node authorization handles kubelet requests, RBAC handles all other API requests. ABAC is an older file-based authorization system. `--anonymous-auth` controls authentication, not authorization. Admission plugins are separate from authorization modes.

questions.question: Pods in your cluster should not be able to access the cloud provider's instance metadata endpoint (169.254.169.254). Which Kubernetes-native control enforces this?
options: Set `hostNetwork: false` in the Pod spec to prevent access to host network interfaces
Apply the `restricted` Pod Security Standard to all namespaces via PodSecurity admission
Set `--cloud-provider=external` on the kubelet to disable instance metadata access
Create a NetworkPolicy with an egress rule blocking traffic to `169.254.169.254/32`
questions.explanation: A NetworkPolicy egress rule blocking traffic to 169.254.169.254/32 is the correct Kubernetes-native control to prevent pods from reaching the cloud metadata endpoint. `hostNetwork: false` prevents pods from using the host's network namespace but does not block specific IP addresses. Pod Security Standards restrict security context settings, not network destinations. The `--cloud-provider` flag changes resource management, not pod network access.

questions.question: An admin is initialising a cluster via `kubeadm init` and needs the API server certificate's SAN list to include the cluster's external DNS hostname so kubectl users can connect via that name without TLS errors. They edit a kubeadm config file before init. Which clusterConfiguration field adds the SAN?
options: `apiServer.certSANs: ["k8s.example.com"]` in the kubeadm ClusterConfiguration — adds the hostname as a Subject Alternative Name when kubeadm generates the apiserver cert
`apiServer.advertiseAddress: k8s.example.com` — sets the bind address; does not add a SAN to the server certificate
`networking.dnsDomain: k8s.example.com` — sets the cluster DNS suffix used inside the cluster; unrelated to apiserver TLS SANs
`controlPlaneEndpoint: k8s.example.com` alone — sets the load-balancer endpoint but does not on its own append a name to the cert's SAN list
questions.explanation: To include custom SANs in the API server certificate during cluster initialization, use the `certSANs` list in the kubeadm `InitConfiguration` under `apiServer`. kubeadm generates the certificate with those SANs included. Manually setting TLS flags after the fact does not add SANs to the existing certificate. TLS Secrets are for Ingress, not the API server itself. `requestheader-extra-headers-prefix` is for aggregation layer auth.

questions.question: You need to expose a service via Ingress with TLS termination using a Kubernetes Secret. Which Secret type and Ingress spec are correct?
options: Secret type `kubernetes.io/tls` with `ca.crt` and `ca.key`; referenced in Ingress `spec.rules[].http`
Secret type `kubernetes.io/tls` with `tls.crt` and `tls.key`; referenced in Ingress `spec.tls[].secretName`
Secret type `kubernetes.io/service-account-token` with the certificate embedded in the token payload
Secret type `Opaque` with `certificate` and `privateKey` keys; referenced in Ingress `spec.tls[].secretName`
questions.explanation: Ingress TLS termination requires a Secret of type `kubernetes.io/tls` containing the standard keys `tls.crt` (certificate) and `tls.key` (private key). The Secret name is referenced in the Ingress spec under `spec.tls[].secretName`. Using `Opaque` with different key names won't work — Ingress controllers expect the standard type. The CA cert and key are used for signing, not for TLS termination. Service account tokens are for API authentication.

questions.question: The CIS Kubernetes Benchmark recommends disabling anonymous authentication on the API server. Which flag achieves this, and what is its effect?
options: `--disable-admission-plugins=NamespaceLifecycle` — prevents anonymous users from creating namespaces
`--insecure-port=0` — closes the plain HTTP port to prevent unauthenticated HTTP access
`--enable-admission-plugins=AlwaysPullImages` — forces all requests to re-authenticate by pulling images
`--anonymous-auth=false` — rejects requests with no credentials instead of mapping them to `system:anonymous`
questions.explanation: `--anonymous-auth=false` prevents the API server from processing requests that arrive without credentials. By default, unauthenticated requests are given the `system:anonymous` identity (group `system:unauthenticated`) and can access public endpoints. With this flag, all requests must authenticate. `--insecure-port=0` closes the legacy HTTP port (good but different). AlwaysPullImages is an admission controller that controls image pull behavior, not authentication.

questions.question: A developer needs to list and get Pods in the `dev` namespace only. Which RBAC configuration correctly implements minimum privilege?
options: Create a Role with `["*"]` verbs on all resources in `dev` and bind it with a RoleBinding
Create a ClusterRole with `["get","list"]` on Pods and bind it with a ClusterRoleBinding to the developer
Create a Role in `dev` with `["get","list"]` on `pods` and bind it to the developer with a RoleBinding
Create a ClusterRole with `["get","list","watch"]` on Pods and bind it with a RoleBinding in `dev`
questions.explanation: Minimum privilege requires a namespace-scoped `Role` (not ClusterRole) in the `dev` namespace granting only the needed verbs (`get` and `list`) on the specific resource (`pods`), bound via a `RoleBinding`. Using a ClusterRole with ClusterRoleBinding grants cluster-wide access. Using `["*"]` grants excessive verbs. A ClusterRole bound via RoleBinding restricts scope to the namespace but `watch` is not required and the ClusterRole itself exists globally.

questions.question: A batch job Pod does not need to communicate with the Kubernetes API. What is the most secure way to ensure no service account token is mounted?
options: Set `automountServiceAccountToken: false` directly in the Pod spec to override the SA-level setting
Set `serviceAccountName: ""` in the Pod spec — an empty name prevents automatic token mounting
Delete the default ServiceAccount in the namespace so no SA can be assigned to the Pod
Set `automountServiceAccountToken: false` on the namespace's default ServiceAccount object
questions.explanation: Setting `automountServiceAccountToken: false` in the Pod spec is the most targeted and reliable approach — it overrides any ServiceAccount-level configuration and applies directly to this Pod. Setting it on the ServiceAccount disables mounting for all pods using that SA (less granular). An empty serviceAccountName is invalid. Deleting the default SA is disruptive and Kubernetes will recreate it.

questions.question: You want to prevent kubelets from modifying Node or Pod objects outside their own scope. Which admission controller enforces this?
options: NodeRestriction — limits kubelets to only modify their own Node object and Pods scheduled on them
AlwaysPullImages — ensures images are re-pulled, preventing kubelets from using cached compromised images
PodSecurity — enforces pod security standards including restrictions on what kubelets can schedule
ResourceQuota — limits compute resources per namespace, preventing rogue kubelets from over-provisioning
questions.explanation: The `NodeRestriction` admission controller restricts each kubelet's API access: it can only read/write its own Node object and the Pod objects that are scheduled on it. This prevents a compromised node from modifying other nodes or pods. PodSecurity enforces security standards on pod specs. AlwaysPullImages controls image caching behavior. ResourceQuota limits resource consumption per namespace.

questions.question: A cluster admin is moving control-plane nodes from v1.29 to v1.30 using kubeadm. Before draining any worker, they run a single kubeadm command on the FIRST control-plane node that validates target compatibility, lists what would change, and recommends component-by-component upgrade order without applying anything. Which command is the correct FIRST step?
options: `kubeadm upgrade plan` — queries the API server for the target version, validates skew and feature-gate rules, and lists the planned upgrade per component WITHOUT making changes
`kubeadm upgrade apply v1.30.0` — directly applies the upgrade to the control-plane node; would skip the recommended dry-run plan step
`kubectl drain node-1 --ignore-daemonsets` — drains workloads, but is performed AFTER planning and before applying, on workers — not the first overall step
`apt-get install kubelet=1.30.0` — installs the new kubelet, which is done LATER and per-node, not as the first plan-stage command
questions.explanation: The correct upgrade order is: (1) upgrade the control plane first with `kubeadm upgrade apply v1.30.x`, (2) for multi-control-plane setups, upgrade remaining control plane nodes with `kubeadm upgrade node`, (3) drain each worker, upgrade kubelet/kubectl on it, uncordon. Worker nodes must be at or below the control plane version — a worker on a newer version than the control plane is unsupported. Parallel upgrades risk version skew and potential downtime. then drain and upgrade each worker node sequentially

questions.question: A microservice needs to read ConfigMaps in `config` namespace and list Deployments in `app` namespace. How do you implement this with least privilege?
options: Create a single Role in the `config` namespace that covers resources in both namespaces
Create two separate Roles (one per namespace) with targeted verbs and bind each with a namespace-scoped RoleBinding
Assign the built-in `view` ClusterRole cluster-wide to ensure the SA can always access what it needs
Create a ClusterRole with permissions on both resources and bind it cluster-wide with a ClusterRoleBinding
questions.explanation: Least privilege requires separate namespace-scoped Roles: one Role in `config` granting only ConfigMap read access, another Role in `app` granting only Deployment list access, each bound with a RoleBinding in the respective namespace. A ClusterRole/ClusterRoleBinding grants cluster-wide access, violating least privilege. A single Role can only govern one namespace. Even the built-in `view` ClusterRole is broader than needed and applies to all namespaces when bound via ClusterRoleBinding.

questions.question: Compliance requires that all Secret read operations are recorded with full request and response payloads. Which audit policy stage and level achieves this?
options: Stage: `RequestReceived`, Level: `Request` — records the request body before the response is sent
Stage: `ResponseComplete`, Level: `RequestResponse` — records full request and response payloads on completion
Stage: `ResponseComplete`, Level: `Metadata` — records request metadata without capturing Secret contents
Stage: `ResponseStarted`, Level: `RequestResponse` — records full payloads when the response starts streaming
questions.explanation: `RequestResponse` level logs both the request object and response object (full payloads). `ResponseComplete` stage fires after the complete response has been sent to the client. This combination captures everything about Secret read operations. `Metadata` only logs request metadata (no body). `Request` logs the request body only. `ResponseStarted` is used for long-running streaming responses (like exec/watch), not standard reads.

questions.question: Your security team requires that no Pod can run with `privileged: true`. Which built-in Kubernetes admission controller (available since 1.25) enforces this?
options: PodSecurity — enforces `baseline` or `restricted` Pod Security Standards, both prohibiting privileged containers
NodeRestriction — prevents nodes from accepting Pods that have privileged security contexts
SecurityContextDeny — a deprecated plugin that blocks Pods with any privileged security context
ValidatingAdmissionWebhook — requires deploying a custom external webhook server to enforce the rule
questions.explanation: The built-in `PodSecurity` admission controller (GA in Kubernetes 1.25) enforces the Pod Security Standards. The `baseline` level prohibits privileged containers; the `restricted` level is even stricter. You apply it by labeling namespaces. `SecurityContextDeny` is a legacy plugin removed in newer Kubernetes versions. `NodeRestriction` controls kubelet API access. `ValidatingAdmissionWebhook` can enforce custom policies but requires an external webhook server — PodSecurity is built-in and preferred.

questions.question: Kubernetes service account tokens have no expiration by default. What mechanism provides time-limited, audience-bound tokens that expire with the Pod?
options: Automatic Secret rotation — Kubernetes rotates ServiceAccount Secret tokens on a defined schedule
RBAC token expiry annotations set on the ServiceAccount object
The TokenRequest API — used by the kubelet to obtain tokens with `expirationSeconds` bound to the Pod's lifetime
OIDC token projection via projected service account volume sources
questions.explanation: The TokenRequest API (GA in Kubernetes 1.21) issues projected service account tokens that are time-limited (via `expirationSeconds`), audience-bound, and automatically invalidated when the Pod is deleted. The kubelet uses the TokenRequest API when mounting tokens into Pods via projected volumes. OIDC projection uses this mechanism under the hood, but the core feature is the TokenRequest API itself. Legacy ServiceAccount Secrets contain long-lived tokens with no expiry.

questions.question: On a hardened control plane, the operator sets `--anonymous-auth=false` on the kube-apiserver. After the API server reloads, requests carrying no credentials are rejected. The `system:anonymous` user is no longer recognised. Which group of users is affected after this flag is set?
options: Any unauthenticated request previously mapped to user `system:anonymous` / group `system:unauthenticated` is now rejected with 401; clients must present a valid token, certificate, or other auth credential
Only service accounts inside the cluster — their JWTs are revoked and they must be re-issued by kube-controller-manager before they can authenticate again
Only nodes — kubelets lose their identity certificates and cannot rejoin the cluster until kubeadm re-issues their client certs
Only external OIDC users — their tokens stop being validated against the configured OIDC issuer, while certificate-based admins are unaffected
questions.explanation: `--anonymous-auth=false` only affects requests that arrive without any credentials. Previously, such requests were mapped to `system:anonymous` user (group `system:unauthenticated`). With this setting, they receive HTTP 401 Unauthorized. Service accounts use JWT projected tokens. Kubelets use TLS client certificates. Admin users use kubeconfig certificates or bearer tokens — none of these are anonymous, so they're unaffected.

questions.question: You want to apply an AppArmor profile named `no-write-etc` (already loaded on the node) to a container. How do you reference it in Kubernetes 1.30+?
options: Set `annotations: {"container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/<name>": "localhost/no-write-etc"}` on the Pod
Create an AppArmorProfile CRD and reference it in `spec.securityContext.appArmorProfile.type`
Set `appArmorProfile.type: Localhost` and `appArmorProfile.localhostProfile: no-write-etc` in the container's `securityContext`
Add `appArmor: no-write-etc` to the container's `securityContext.capabilities` field
questions.explanation: In Kubernetes 1.30+, AppArmor is configured in the container `securityContext` using `appArmorProfile.type: Localhost` and `appArmorProfile.localhostProfile` pointing to the profile name already loaded on the node. The annotation-based approach (`container.apparmor.security.beta.kubernetes.io/`) is the legacy method (pre-1.30, still works but deprecated). AppArmor profiles are not part of Linux capabilities. There is no AppArmorProfile CRD in standard Kubernetes.

questions.question: You want a container to use the `RuntimeDefault` seccomp profile to restrict its allowed syscalls. Which Pod spec achieves this in Kubernetes 1.27+?
options: Create a SeccompProfile CRD referencing the default profile and apply it via an admission webhook
Set `seccompProfile.type: Unconfined` — this applies the runtime's default profile
Set `annotations: {"seccomp.security.alpha.kubernetes.io/pod": "docker/default"}` on the Pod
Set `seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault` in the container's or Pod's `securityContext`
questions.explanation: The correct modern approach (Kubernetes 1.22+) is to set `securityContext.seccompProfile.type: RuntimeDefault` in the container or Pod spec. This applies whatever the container runtime defines as its default seccomp filter. The annotation-based method (`seccomp.security.alpha.kubernetes.io`) is the legacy approach (deprecated). `Unconfined` explicitly disables seccomp filtering — the opposite of what is needed. There is no SeccompProfile CRD in standard Kubernetes.

questions.question: A security engineer is hardening worker nodes against the CIS Kubernetes Benchmark. They want the set of actions that aligns with the benchmark's node-level recommendations covering kubelet flags, file permissions on kubeconfig and PKI, and disabling read-only ports. Which set of actions fits?
options: Enable `--anonymous-auth=false` and `--authorization-mode=Webhook` on kubelet, set strict 0600 perms on kubeconfig and PKI files, disable the kubelet read-only port (10255), and audit /var/lib/kubelet
Open the kubelet read-only port to all subnets so monitoring scrapes can succeed, and grant 0666 to /etc/kubernetes/admin.conf for ease of use across SRE machines
Disable TLS on the kubelet so cAdvisor metrics can be scraped without cert management, and grant `system:anonymous` view access to ease debugging in production
Run all kubelets as root with `--read-only-port=10255` enabled, and keep PKI files world-readable on every node to avoid permission errors during incident response
questions.explanation: CIS benchmarks recommend minimizing the OS footprint: uninstall packages not needed for Kubernetes, disable or unload unnecessary kernel modules (`dccp`, `sctp`, `rds`, etc.), ensure only required services are running, and keep the system patched. Installing all packages increases the attack surface. Enabling all kernel modules provides more exploitation vectors. Running services as root violates the principle of least privilege.

questions.question: You need to permanently prevent the `dccp` kernel module from loading on a Kubernetes node. Which configuration achieves persistent blacklisting?
options: `modprobe -r dccp && echo "blacklist dccp" >> /etc/modules` — removes and adds to load list
`systemctl disable dccp && systemctl stop dccp` — disables the dccp service at boot
Add `blacklist dccp` to a file under `/etc/modprobe.d/` (e.g., `kubernetes-blacklist.conf`) and reboot
`rmmod dccp && echo "install dccp /bin/false" >> /etc/modules` — removes and marks for auto-load
questions.explanation: To persistently blacklist a kernel module, add `blacklist dccp` to a file in `/etc/modprobe.d/` such as `/etc/modprobe.d/kubernetes-blacklist.conf`. You can also add `install dccp /bin/false` to prevent loading even when explicitly requested. A reboot applies the change. `modprobe -r` only unloads for the current session. `/etc/modules` lists modules to LOAD at boot, not blacklist. `systemctl` manages services, not kernel modules.

questions.question: A container escapes and needs root on the host. Which kernel feature in Kubernetes 1.30+, when enabled, limits the blast radius by mapping container UID 0 to an unprivileged host UID?
options: Seccomp `RuntimeDefault` profile — filters syscalls that could escalate privileges to the host
AppArmor profiles — restrict file system paths that could be used for privilege escalation
User namespaces (`hostUsers: false`) — remaps container UIDs to unprivileged host UIDs (e.g., 100000+)
Pod Security Admission `restricted` profile — forces `runAsNonRoot: true` preventing root in containers
questions.explanation: User namespaces (`hostUsers: false` in the Pod spec, Kubernetes 1.30 stable) remap the container's root UID (0) to a high non-root host UID (100000+). If a container escapes, the process has no special privileges on the host — it's an unprivileged user. Seccomp and AppArmor reduce the attack surface but don't prevent host-level privileges if root escapes. `runAsNonRoot` prevents root inside the container but doesn't change the host UID mapping.

questions.question: A container needs to bind to port 80 but must not have any other elevated privileges. Which SecurityContext configuration is correct?
options: Use `capabilities.drop: ["ALL"]` then `capabilities.add: ["NET_BIND_SERVICE"]` to add only what is needed
Set `privileged: true` to enable all capabilities including the one needed for port binding
Set `runAsUser: 0` since only root can bind to ports below 1024
Set `capabilities.add: ["ALL"]` which implicitly includes NET_BIND_SERVICE
questions.explanation: The principle of least privilege: drop ALL capabilities first with `capabilities.drop: ["ALL"]`, then add back only `NET_BIND_SERVICE` which grants the ability to bind to ports below 1024 without root. `privileged: true` grants every capability plus disables all isolation — a critical security risk. `capabilities.add: ["ALL"]` grants every privilege. Running as root (UID 0) is a bad practice when a specific capability suffices.

questions.question: You want to prevent a container from gaining additional privileges via setuid/setgid binaries or file capabilities. Which SecurityContext field achieves this?
options: Set `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` — prevents any new binaries from being written to the filesystem
Set `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false` — sets the `no_new_privs` bit preventing privilege escalation
Set `capabilities.drop: ["SETUID","SETGID"]` — removes the setuid and setgid capabilities
Set `runAsNonRoot: true` — prevents the process from running as root UID 0
questions.explanation: `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false` sets the Linux `no_new_privs` bit on the process. This prevents processes from gaining privileges through setuid/setgid executables or file capabilities, even if such binaries exist in the image. It's distinct from capabilities — it's a process flag. `readOnlyRootFilesystem` prevents filesystem writes. `runAsNonRoot` controls the user identity. Dropping SETUID/SETGID capabilities is related but `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false` is the direct control for the `no_new_privs` mechanism.

questions.question: A team wants to prevent attackers who land remote code execution from installing extra tools (curl, nc, bash utilities) inside containers, by making the container filesystem read-only at runtime. Application data goes through explicit writable mounts. Which SecurityContext setting enforces this?
options: `securityContext.readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` — mounts the container's root filesystem read-only at runtime; writes are limited to explicitly mounted writable volumes
`securityContext.allowPrivilegeEscalation: false` — blocks setuid escalation, but leaves the root filesystem writable for tool installation
`securityContext.capabilities.drop: ["ALL"]` — strips Linux capabilities; reduces blast radius but does not prevent writes by a user with normal file permissions
`securityContext.runAsNonRoot: true` — forces a non-root UID; non-root users can still write to user-owned paths inside the container filesystem
questions.explanation: `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` mounts the container's root filesystem as read-only, so any write attempt — including installing tools, dropping backdoors, or modifying configuration — is rejected. Applications that need writable areas should use `emptyDir` or other volumes for specific directories. Seccomp can block some syscalls but `readOnlyRootFilesystem` is the direct and complete filesystem immutability control.

questions.question: Which Pod spec setting represents the MOST dangerous privilege escalation risk and should always be avoided in production?
options: `spec.hostNetwork: true` — allows the Pod to access all host network interfaces
`spec.containers[].securityContext.privileged: true`.
`spec.containers[].securityContext.runAsUser: 0` — runs the container process as root
`spec.hostPID: true` — allows the Pod to see all processes running on the host
questions.explanation: `privileged: true` is the most dangerous setting. It effectively disables all cgroup and Linux namespace isolation for the container, grants every Linux capability, and allows access to all host devices. This is equivalent to running a process as root directly on the host — a full container escape. While `hostPID: true` and `hostNetwork: true` are serious risks confined to specific namespaces, `privileged: true` removes ALL isolation. Even running as root (UID 0) inside a normal container is less dangerous. disables all container isolation and grants all capabilities

questions.question: Pod Security Admission is set to `restricted` on the `payments` namespace. A Pod fails because its image runs as root (UID 0). What is the correct fix?
options: Delete the LimitRange object in the namespace since it is enforcing the non-root requirement
Add label `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: baseline` to relax the namespace to baseline standard
Add `privileged: true` to the container `securityContext` to allow root processes under the restricted profile
Add `runAsNonRoot: true` and `runAsUser: 1000` to the container `securityContext`,.
questions.explanation: The `restricted` Pod Security Standard requires containers to run as non-root. The correct fix is to configure `securityContext.runAsNonRoot: true` (and optionally `runAsUser: 1000` or another non-zero UID), or rebuild the image with a `USER` directive pointing to a non-root user. Changing the namespace label to `baseline` would relax security. `privileged: true` is blocked by both `baseline` and `restricted` profiles. LimitRange controls resource consumption, not security contexts. or rebuild the image with a non-root USER directive

questions.question: You want to use OPA Gatekeeper to prevent Pods from using the `latest` image tag cluster-wide. Which Gatekeeper resources are required?
options: A single `Policy` object with a Rego rule checking `input.review.object.spec.containers[_].image`
A `ConstraintTemplate` defining the Rego logic and a `Constraint` object (an instance of the template) applied to Pods
A `ValidatingWebhookConfiguration` pointing directly to a Rego policy file stored on disk
A `ClusterRole` that denies the `create` verb on Pods when images use the `latest` tag
questions.explanation: OPA Gatekeeper requires two resources: (1) a `ConstraintTemplate` — a CRD that defines the Rego policy logic, (2) a `Constraint` — an instance of that CRD that activates the policy with specific scope and parameters (like `kinds: [Pod]` and excluded namespaces). Gatekeeper manages its own ValidatingWebhookConfiguration internally — you don't create it directly. There is no standalone `Policy` object in Gatekeeper. RBAC cannot inspect Pod field values like image tags.

questions.question: Your security team requires that Secret values never appear in `kubectl describe pod` output or in process environment dumps. Which approach best achieves this?
options: Mount the Secret as a volume file and access it programmatically, avoiding environment variable exposure
Store the secret in a ConfigMap with `immutable: true` since ConfigMaps are encrypted at rest by default
Use `env[].valueFrom.secretKeyRef` to selectively load specific secret values as environment variables
Use `envFrom: secretRef` to load all secret keys as environment variables from the Secret
questions.explanation: Mounting Secrets as volume files is more secure than environment variables. Both `envFrom` and `valueFrom.secretKeyRef` expose values in `kubectl describe pod` output (they appear in the env section) and in process environment dumps (`/proc/<pid>/environ`). Volume-mounted Secret files are not shown in pod descriptions and are harder to accidentally leak. ConfigMaps are not encrypted at rest and are not intended for sensitive data.

questions.question: A regulated environment requires stronger isolation than the default container runtime provides for untrusted workloads. Which Kubernetes feature enables using an alternative runtime like gVisor or Kata Containers?
options: Create a PodDisruptionBudget to protect the Pod from deletion during security scans
Use a `SecurityContext` with `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` and `privileged: false` for sandbox isolation
Create a `RuntimeClass` resource and reference it via `spec.runtimeClassName` in the Pod spec
Set `spec.hostPID: false` and `spec.hostNetwork: false` — removing host privileges enables sandbox mode
questions.explanation: `RuntimeClass` allows specifying which container runtime handler to use for a Pod. By creating a RuntimeClass referencing the gVisor (`runsc`) or Kata Containers handler, and setting `spec.runtimeClassName` in the Pod, that Pod runs with the alternative runtime providing stronger kernel isolation. `hostPID/hostNetwork: false` just removes host namespace access from the default runtime. PodDisruptionBudgets control availability. SecurityContext hardening operates within the default runtime.

questions.question: You want `production` namespace to deny non-compliant Pods, `staging` to warn, and `development` to audit-log violations. Which namespace labels achieve this?
options: `production`: `pod-security.kubernetes.io/mode: enforce`; `staging`: `pod-security.kubernetes.io/mode: warn`; `development`: `pod-security.kubernetes.io/mode: audit`
Set `PodSecurity=true` in the kube-apiserver feature gates and apply `mode` labels directly to Pods
Apply a single ClusterPolicy with `enforce: restricted, warn: baseline, audit: baseline` across all namespaces
`production`: `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted`; `staging`: `pod-security.kubernetes.io/warn: baseline`;.
questions.explanation: Pod Security Admission uses namespace labels with the format `pod-security.kubernetes.io/<mode>: <level>`. Modes are `enforce` (reject non-compliant Pods), `warn` (allow but warn), and `audit` (allow but log). Levels are `privileged`, `baseline`, and `restricted`. The `mode` key does not exist as a standalone label. There is no ClusterPolicy object in built-in Pod Security Admission. The feature is enabled by default since Kubernetes 1.23. `development`: `pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit: baseline`

questions.question: You need to scan the `nginx:1.25` image for CRITICAL severity CVEs and fail the CI pipeline if any are found. Which Trivy command achieves this?
options: `trivy image --severity CRITICAL --exit-code 1 nginx:1.25`
`trivy scan image=nginx:1.25 severity=CRITICAL fail=true`
`trivy container nginx:1.25 --threshold CRITICAL --exit 1`
`trivy image nginx:1.25 --level CRITICAL --fail-on-critical`
questions.explanation: The correct Trivy command is `trivy image --severity CRITICAL --exit-code 1 nginx:1.25`. The `--exit-code 1` flag causes Trivy to exit with code 1 when vulnerabilities of the specified severity are found, making CI/CD pipelines fail. `--severity CRITICAL` filters results to only show CRITICAL CVEs. The other options use invalid flags: `--level`, `--fail-on-critical`, `--threshold` do not exist in Trivy's CLI. `trivy container` and `trivy scan` are not valid subcommands.

questions.question: You have installed gVisor (`runsc`) on worker nodes and configured containerd with handler `runsc`. Which YAML creates the correct RuntimeClass?
options: `apiVersion: apps/v1 / kind: RuntimeClass / metadata: {name: gvisor} / spec: {runtime: runsc}`
`apiVersion: node.k8s.io/v1 / kind: RuntimeClass / metadata: {name: gvisor} / handler: runsc`
`apiVersion: node.k8s.io/v1beta1 / kind: RuntimeClass / spec: {runtimeHandler: runsc} / metadata: {name: gvisor}`
`apiVersion: v1 / kind: RuntimeClass / metadata: {name: gvisor} / handler: runsc`
questions.explanation: RuntimeClass uses `apiVersion: node.k8s.io/v1` (stable since Kubernetes 1.20). The `handler` field is at the top level of the spec (not inside a nested `spec` block) and points to the container runtime handler name (e.g., `runsc` for gVisor). The v1beta1 API used `spec.runtimeHandler` — the stable v1 API uses just `handler` at root. Using `apps/v1` is incorrect. The `v1` core API group doesn't include RuntimeClass.

questions.question: After labeling `prod` namespace with `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: restricted`, existing Pods fail. You need to identify violations before enforcing. Which approach is least disruptive?
options: Set `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: privileged` to allow all Pods while you audit
Set `pod-security.kubernetes.io/audit: restricted` to log violations to the audit log without blocking Pods
Set `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce: baseline` as a stepping stone to `restricted`
Set `pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce-version: latest` to use the latest standard without blocking
questions.explanation: Using `audit` mode logs violations to the Kubernetes audit log without rejecting any Pods. This is the least disruptive first step — it lets you identify which workloads need changes before enforcing. After fixing violations, switch to `warn` to see real-time warnings in API responses, then finally `enforce`. Setting `privileged` defeats the purpose. `enforce-version` is a label variant that controls which version of the standard is used (e.g., `v1.29`), not the strictness. `enforce: baseline` may be a useful intermediate step but `audit` is non-blocking.

questions.question: An attacker obtained a Kubernetes Secret. The external token has been rotated but the old Secret object still exists. What is the complete remediation?
options: Delete the old Secret and recreate it with the new value;.
Update the Secret's `immutable: true` field to prevent further modification or exposure
Use `kubectl patch secret <name> -p '{"data": null}'` to wipe the Secret data without deleting it
Update `metadata.resourceVersion` in the Secret spec to force Kubernetes to refresh the Secret
questions.explanation: The correct remediation is: delete the old Secret, recreate it with the new value. For Pods using it as an environment variable, a rolling restart is required since env vars are baked in at Pod start. For volume-mounted Secrets, Kubernetes automatically refreshes them within the kubelet's sync period (default ~1 minute). `kubectl patch` with null data would corrupt the Secret. Setting `immutable: true` prevents future updates. `metadata.resourceVersion` is managed by Kubernetes and cannot be set manually. rollout-restart Deployments using it as env var (volume-mounted Secrets auto-refresh within the kubelet sync period)

questions.question: A cluster stores Kubernetes Secrets in etcd with default base64 encoding only. The security team wants secrets to be encrypted at rest in etcd using a KMS- or AES-CBC-backed provider configured through an EncryptionConfiguration. How is this enabled?
options: Create an `EncryptionConfiguration` referencing `secrets` resources with a KMS provider or `aescbc`, pass `--encryption-provider-config=<file>` to kube-apiserver, then re-create or rewrite existing Secrets to apply encryption
Add the annotation `encryption: true` to each Secret manifest; the API server will encrypt those entries individually while leaving the rest base64-encoded
Set `etcd.dataEncryption: true` in the kubeadm ClusterConfiguration; etcd then performs application-layer encryption without API-server involvement
Enable `--allow-privileged=false` on kube-apiserver; this implicitly turns on encryption-at-rest for all resources stored in the cluster's etcd backend
questions.explanation: Encryption at rest requires an `EncryptionConfiguration` YAML file that specifies the encryption provider (e.g., `aescbc`, `secretbox`, or `aesgcm`) and the key, then pass `--encryption-provider-config=<path>` to the kube-apiserver. This only encrypts newly written Secrets — existing ones must be re-written: `kubectl get secrets -A -o json | kubectl replace -f -`. The `--encryption-provider-config` flag is for the kube-apiserver, not kubelet. There is no `SecretEncryption` feature gate or `--encrypt` flag. pass it to kube-apiserver with `--encryption-provider-config`

questions.question: Your organization uses HashiCorp Vault. Which approach integrates Vault with Kubernetes Pods without storing the actual secret value in a Kubernetes Secret object?
options: Use the Vault Agent Injector sidecar to dynamically deliver secrets to Pods without creating Kubernetes Secret objects
Store secrets in a ConfigMap with Vault encryption annotations to prevent etcd exposure
Use the Vault CSI driver to mount Vault secrets as ephemeral volumes directly into Pods
Mount a Vault token as a Kubernetes Secret and use it in Pod env vars to fetch secrets at runtime
questions.explanation: The Vault Agent Injector uses a mutating admission webhook to inject a Vault Agent sidecar into Pods. The sidecar authenticates to Vault using the Pod's service account (via Kubernetes auth) and writes secrets to a shared in-memory volume. No Kubernetes Secret object is created. The Vault CSI driver (option B) also avoids creating Kubernetes Secrets and is another valid approach. Mounting a Vault token as a Kubernetes Secret still puts a sensitive value in Kubernetes. ConfigMaps don't support encryption annotations.

questions.question: A developer asks why Kubernetes Secrets are not truly secure by default. What is the most accurate explanation?
options: Secrets are transmitted in plaintext over HTTP between the kube-apiserver and etcd
Secrets are only base64-encoded (not encrypted) in etcd by default — base64 is trivially reversible
Secrets are encrypted with AES-256 in etcd but the encryption key is stored in the same etcd database
Secrets are readable by any Pod in the namespace since RBAC is not applied to Secret resources
questions.explanation: By default, Kubernetes stores Secrets in etcd as base64-encoded values — base64 is an encoding scheme, not encryption. Anyone with direct etcd access can `base64 -d` to retrieve the value. This is why encryption at rest (EncryptionConfiguration) and external secrets managers are recommended for production. The API server communicates with etcd over TLS (not HTTP). RBAC is enforced for Secrets. The concern is etcd at-rest storage, not AES key placement.

questions.question: You are building a Go binary container image. Which Dockerfile pattern produces the smallest, most secure final image?
options: Use `FROM golang:1.22-alpine` and run the binary directly since Alpine is minimal enough
Multi-stage build: compile in `golang:1.22` builder stage,.
Single `FROM ubuntu:22.04` stage with `RUN apt-get install golang && go build` in one layer
Single `FROM alpine:latest` with `RUN apk add go && go build && apk del go` to remove build tools
questions.explanation: Multi-stage builds produce minimal secure images: compile in a full build environment (`golang:1.22`), then copy only the compiled static binary to `FROM scratch` (no OS at all) or `FROM gcr.io/distroless/static` (minimal OS). The final image has no compiler, no shell, no package manager — drastically reducing the attack surface. Alpine with removing packages still leaves residual build artifacts and is not as minimal as distroless/scratch. `golang:1.22-alpine` includes the entire Go toolchain. copy only the binary to `FROM scratch` or `distroless/static`

questions.question: You want to statically analyze a Pod YAML manifest for security risks before applying it to the cluster. Which tool evaluates Kubernetes resource security and returns an advisory score?
options: `trivy fs --security-checks config pod.yaml` — scans the YAML file for CVEs in referenced images
`kube-score score pod.yaml` — checks YAML syntax and validates against the Kubernetes API schema
`hadolint pod.yaml` — lints the manifest for Docker security best practices
`kubesec scan pod.yaml` — evaluates Kubernetes Pod YAML for security risks with an advisory score
questions.explanation: `kubesec` is specifically designed to scan Kubernetes resource YAML for security risks. It evaluates settings like privileged containers, hostPath volumes, capabilities, and missing securityContext fields — returning a score with risk advisories. `trivy fs` with config scanning checks IaC misconfigurations but uses different rules. `kube-score` focuses on Kubernetes best practices (liveness probes, resource limits) rather than a security advisory score. `hadolint` is a Dockerfile linter, not for Kubernetes YAML.

questions.question: Your team uses Sigstore Cosign to sign images. Which command verifies that `registry.example.com/myapp:v1.0` was signed with your key?
options: `cosign check --signature cosign.sig registry.example.com/myapp:v1.0`
`cosign attach signature --key cosign.pub registry.example.com/myapp:v1.0`
`cosign verify --key cosign.pub registry.example.com/myapp:v1.0`
`cosign sign --key cosign.key registry.example.com/myapp:v1.0`
questions.explanation: `cosign verify --key cosign.pub <image>` verifies the image signature stored in the registry against the public key. The signature is stored as an OCI artifact in the registry alongside the image, written during `cosign sign`. `cosign sign` creates the signature (signing, not verifying). `cosign attach` attaches existing artifacts (SBOMs, signatures) — it doesn't verify. There is no `cosign check` subcommand.

questions.question: You want to prevent Pods from pulling images from registries other than `registry.example.com`. Which approach enforces this cluster-wide?
options: Create an RBAC ClusterRole that denies `create` on Pods with images from other registries
Set `ALLOWED_REGISTRIES=registry.example.com` in the kube-apiserver environment variables
Configure `imagePullSecrets` in all namespaces pointing only to `registry.example.com`
Deploy OPA Gatekeeper with a ConstraintTemplate that checks container image prefixes against the allowed registry
questions.explanation: OPA Gatekeeper (or Kyverno) with a ConstraintTemplate can enforce image registry policies by examining `input.review.object.spec.containers[_].image` during admission and denying any image that doesn't start with the approved registry prefix. There is no kube-apiserver env var for allowed registries. RBAC evaluates verb/resource combinations but cannot inspect Pod field values like image names. `imagePullSecrets` provides credentials for pulling from a registry but does not prevent pulling from other registries.

questions.question: A platform team is choosing a base image for production Go services. They evaluate `gcr.io/distroless/static`, which contains a CA bundle, /etc/passwd, and the runtime libraries needed by their static binary — but NO shell, package manager, or general tools. What is the primary security advantage of using such a distroless base image?
options: Distroless images significantly reduce the attack surface — no shell, package manager, or general OS tools — so post-exploit tool-installation, shell-spawn, and pivot techniques have nothing to operate against inside the container
Distroless images automatically run as a non-root user without any uid configuration in the Pod spec, even on workloads that explicitly request root
Distroless images perform automatic CVE patching at runtime, eliminating the need for periodic image rebuilds in the team's CI/CD pipeline
Distroless images are signed by a Kubernetes signing authority at build time, so admission controllers do not need to verify their provenance
questions.explanation: Distroless images strip everything except the application binary and its direct runtime dependencies. No bash, no sh, no curl, no apt, no package manager. This dramatically limits what an attacker can do if they gain code execution — no tooling for pivoting, exploring, or exfiltrating data. They don't automatically configure seccomp/AppArmor (those are Kubernetes controls). Some variants are signed but that's not their primary security benefit. Non-root execution depends on which distroless variant is used. no shell, no package manager, no debugging tools — minimizing the attack surface on compromise

questions.question: You write a Gatekeeper ConstraintTemplate to block images not from `registry.internal/`. Which Rego expression is correct for Gatekeeper?
options: `deny[msg] { not startswith(input.review.object.spec.containers[_].image, "registry.internal/") }`
`block[msg] { image := input.spec.containers[_].image; contains(image, "registry.internal") == false }`
`deny { spec := input.review.object.spec; every c in spec.containers { not startswith(c.image, "registry.internal/") } }`
`violation[{"msg": msg}] { container := input.review.object.spec.containers[_]; not startswith(container.image.
questions.explanation: Gatekeeper ConstraintTemplates use `violation[{"msg": msg}]` (not `deny` or `block`). The input path is `input.review.object.spec.containers`. Each violation must produce an object with a `msg` key. `startswith` checks the string prefix. Option A uses `deny` which is not Gatekeeper syntax. Option C uses `block` (invalid) and `input.spec` (wrong path — missing `review.object`). Option D uses `deny` and OPA's `every` keyword, which is not used in Gatekeeper's violation pattern. "registry.internal/"); msg := sprintf("image %v not allowed", [container.image]) }`

questions.question: You deploy a mutating admission webhook that injects sidecars into Pods. The webhook becomes temporarily unreachable. How do you prevent this from breaking Pod creation cluster-wide?
options: Set `failurePolicy: Fail` in the MutatingWebhookConfiguration to immediately surface the outage in alerts
Set `namespaceSelector` to limit webhook scope so it doesn't apply to all namespaces
Set `failurePolicy: Ignore` so webhook failures don't block Pod creation
Delete the MutatingWebhookConfiguration and rely on the webhook's own error handling to recover
questions.explanation: `failurePolicy: Ignore` means if the webhook is unreachable or times out, the admission request is allowed to proceed without mutation. This prevents an outage in the webhook from cascading into a cluster-wide inability to create Pods. `failurePolicy: Fail` causes all Pod creations to fail when the webhook is down — dangerous for production workloads. `namespaceSelector` reduces scope but doesn't solve availability. Deleting the webhook removes the sidecar injection functionality entirely.

questions.question: You want to scan all running container images in the Kubernetes cluster for HIGH and CRITICAL CVEs. Which Trivy command does this?
options: `trivy image --scan-all-nodes --severity HIGH,CRITICAL`
`trivy k8s --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --report all cluster`
`trivy kubernetes --namespace all --severity HIGH,CRITICAL pods`
`trivy cluster --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --output report.html`
questions.explanation: `trivy k8s` is the subcommand for scanning Kubernetes clusters. The `--report all` flag outputs all findings, and `cluster` scans the entire cluster. The full command `trivy k8s --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --report all cluster` scans all running images. `--scan-all-nodes` is not a valid flag. `trivy kubernetes` is not a valid subcommand (use `trivy k8s`). `trivy cluster` does not exist.

questions.question: During a security audit, you must produce a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) for `nginx:1.25` in CycloneDX format. Which Trivy command achieves this?
options: `trivy image --format cyclonedx nginx:1.25`
`trivy image nginx:1.25 --sbom cyclonedx --output sbom.json`
`trivy scan --sbom --format cyclonedx --target nginx:1.25`
`trivy sbom generate --image nginx:1.25 --output cyclonedx`
questions.explanation: `trivy image --format cyclonedx <image>` generates a CycloneDX-format SBOM for the container image. Trivy supports multiple SBOM formats: `cyclonedx`, `spdx`, `spdx-json`, and `github`. There is no `trivy sbom generate` subcommand — use `trivy image` with the format flag. `--sbom` is not a valid Trivy flag. `trivy scan` is not a valid subcommand in modern Trivy versions.

questions.question: A Deployment needs to pull from a private registry requiring authentication. How do you configure this securely without hardcoding credentials in the Deployment spec?
options: Mount Docker credentials as a ConfigMap at `/etc/docker/registry.json` in each container
Create a Secret of type `kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson` and reference it in `spec.imagePullSecrets` in the Pod spec
Add registry credentials to `/root/.docker/config.json` on all worker nodes and they will be auto-detected by kubelet
Set env vars `REGISTRY_USER` and `REGISTRY_PASSWORD` in the container spec — kubelet reads these for image pulls
questions.explanation: Create a Secret of type `kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson` with the registry credentials, then reference it in `spec.imagePullSecrets` in the Pod spec (or on the namespace's ServiceAccount for automatic application). Configuring credentials on nodes is node-specific and not portable or scalable. Env vars are not read by the kubelet for image pulls. ConfigMaps are not the right resource type for credentials and are not encrypted.

questions.question: You integrate vulnerability scanning into your CI pipeline. At which stage should scanning occur for maximum security impact?
options: At deploy time — use an admission webhook to scan images during Pod admission
After pushing to the registry — scan the pushed tag via a webhook triggered by the registry push event
Before pushing to the registry.
After deploying to production — scan running Pods with `trivy k8s` to catch runtime CVEs
questions.explanation: The earliest intervention point for maximum security is scanning in CI before pushing to the registry. This prevents vulnerable images from ever entering the supply chain. Post-push scanning (option B) is better than post-deploy but still allows the image into the registry. Runtime scanning (option A) is reactive and has high latency. Admission webhook scanning (option D) is a defense-in-depth layer but catches issues very late — use it in addition to, not instead of, CI scanning. scan the locally built image in CI and fail the build before it can be pushed

questions.question: You configure an `ImagePolicyWebhook` with `defaultAllow: false`. The webhook server goes down. What happens to new Pod creation requests?
options: Kubernetes falls back to allowing all images since the webhook is unavailable (fail-open)
All new Pod creation requests are denied until the webhook server becomes available again (fail-closed)
Only Pods in `kube-system` are allowed through; Pods in other namespaces are blocked
The API server caches the last webhook result and uses it until the server recovers
questions.explanation: `defaultAllow: false` implements fail-closed behavior: if the ImagePolicyWebhook server is unreachable, the admission request is denied. This is the secure default for security enforcement — you don't want unscanned images to bypass the policy when the scanner is unavailable. `defaultAllow: true` would fail-open, allowing all images during an outage. There is no caching behavior or namespace-based fallback in the ImagePolicyWebhook.

questions.question: You want a Falco rule to alert when a process inside any container reads `/etc/shadow`. Which rule condition is correct?
options: `syscall.type=read and file.path=/etc/shadow and kubernetes.namespace != ""`
`read_file and container and filename contains "/etc/shadow" and evt.args contains "shadow"`
`open_read and container and fd.name=/etc/shadow`
`evt.type=openat and container.id != "" and path.file="/etc/shadow"`
questions.explanation: `open_read` is a Falco macro matching file-open events for reading. `container` is the Falco macro that restricts events to container context. `fd.name` is the file descriptor name (full path). This combination correctly fires when any container reads `/etc/shadow`. Option B uses non-existent Falco fields (`syscall.type`, `file.path`, `kubernetes.namespace`). Option C uses `path.file` (invalid; should be `fd.name`). Option D uses `read_file` and `filename` which are not standard Falco macros or fields.

questions.question: Your audit policy generates too many low-value events. How do you suppress `get`, `list`, and `watch` requests for ConfigMaps?
options: Set the `configmaps` API group to `Ignore` in the audit backend webhook configuration
Add `level: None; verbs: ["get","list","watch"]; resources: [{group: "", resources: ["configmaps"]}]` at the END of the audit policy
Add `level: None; verbs: ["get","list","watch"];.
Set `omitStages: ["RequestReceived"]` globally in the audit policy to skip pre-response logging
questions.explanation: Kubernetes audit policies are evaluated top-to-bottom, first match wins. To suppress ConfigMap read events, the `level: None` rule MUST be placed BEFORE any broader rules (e.g., `level: Metadata` for all resources), or the broader rule will match first and the None rule will never fire. If placed at the end, it has no effect. `omitStages: [RequestReceived]` only omits that one stage; the response stage is still logged. Audit backends don't have per-resource ignore settings. resources: [{group: "", resources: ["configmaps"]}]` BEFORE any broader-scope rules

questions.question: A team enforcing immutable container infrastructure wants three properties combined: container filesystems must not be writable at runtime, application code never lands inside running containers, and rollouts replace pods rather than mutate them. Which combination best aligns with the immutable-infrastructure model?
options: Set `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true`, bake all code + dependencies into the image at build time, and roll out new versions by replacing pods (rolling/canary) rather than execing into them
Allow writable root filesystems but mount /var/log read-only, push code via `kubectl cp` into running pods, and restart containers rather than recreating pods
Disable image registries entirely and let nodes pull source code from Git on every startup, building binaries on-demand inside the container before serving traffic
Mount /opt as a hostPath read-write so operators can patch binaries quickly on production hosts during incident response, with no image rebuild
questions.explanation: `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` makes the container root filesystem read-only at the OS level — any write attempt returns an error. Applications requiring writable directories (temp files, logs, cache) should mount `emptyDir` volumes for those specific paths. `imagePullPolicy: Always` ensures fresh images on each restart but doesn't prevent filesystem changes at runtime. `lifecycle` hooks run inside the container and can't reliably lock the filesystem. `terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 0` is about pod termination speed, not immutability.

questions.question: A team runs Falco as a runtime threat detector in their cluster. They want every alert pushed to Slack in real time without writing custom code. Which configuration achieves this?
options: Run Falcosidekick (or a similar Falco output forwarder) alongside Falco, configure its Slack webhook URL, and route Falco alerts to it via `program_output` or HTTP output
Configure Falco's `outputs.rate` to 0 and rely on Kubernetes events; the Kubernetes event stream propagates Falco rules into Slack automatically
Patch Falco's source to embed the Slack webhook directly; this is the only supported way to integrate Falco with Slack in a production cluster
Disable Falco's syscall driver and instead schedule a CronJob that re-runs Falco rules against historical logs every hour, posting summaries to Slack
questions.explanation: `falcosidekick` is the standard solution for routing Falco alerts to external services (Slack, PagerDuty, Teams, Elasticsearch, etc.). It receives Falco events via HTTP or gRPC and forwards them. There is no built-in Slack output in Falco itself. `json_output: true` writes JSON to stdout/file but doesn't push to Slack. There is no `--output slack_webhook_url` CLI flag. Slack URLs are not configured inside rule definitions.

questions.question: You want to stream Kubernetes audit logs to an external SIEM in near-real time. Which audit backend achieves this?
options: Dynamic backend (`--audit-dynamic-configuration`) — allows runtime configuration of audit sinks
Kafka backend (`--audit-kafka-config`) — streams audit events directly to a Kafka topic
Webhook backend (`--audit-webhook-config-file`).
Log backend (`--audit-log-path`) — writes audit events to a file that a SIEM log shipper agent tails
questions.explanation: The webhook audit backend (`--audit-webhook-config-file`) sends audit events to an external HTTP endpoint in near-real time via POST requests. This can point to a SIEM ingestion endpoint or a log forwarder. The log backend writes to files (suitable for local collection agents but with more latency). The dynamic audit configuration was deprecated and removed in Kubernetes 1.27. There is no native Kafka audit backend in Kubernetes. POSTs audit events to an external HTTP endpoint in near-real time

questions.question: A SOC analyst writes a Falco rule that should fire whenever an attacker drops into an interactive shell inside a running container (`docker exec` / `kubectl exec` followed by /bin/bash). Which Falco condition expression best detects this behaviour?
options: `spawned_process and container and proc.name in (bash, sh, zsh, ksh, dash) and proc.tty != 0` — matches a shell binary launched inside a container on a tty, which is the typical exec-into-pod fingerprint
`evt.type = open and fd.name startswith /etc/passwd` — detects passwd-file reads but not shell spawns; wrong syscall family for the use case
`container.image.repository contains alpine` — matches by image name only, with no behavioural component; will fire on every alpine workload start
`k8s.ns.name = kube-system and proc.name = kubelet` — matches normal kubelet activity in kube-system, an expected baseline behaviour rather than an exec event
questions.explanation: The standard Falco condition for detecting shell spawning uses `spawned_process` (macro for execve events), `container` (macro scoping to container context), `proc.name in (sh, bash, zsh, dash)` to match known shells, and excludes container runtime parents to reduce false positives from the container lifecycle. `fd.name endswith "/bin/sh"` checks a file descriptor path, not the spawned process name. `proc.cmdline` can work but is less reliable. `shell_spawn` is not a standard Falco macro. bash, zsh, dash) and not proc.pname in (runc, containerd)`

questions.question: A security incident requires identifying which user deleted a Secret in the `prod` namespace. Which audit log fields provide this information?
options: `user.username`, `verb`, `objectRef.namespace`.
`annotations.authorization.k8s.io/reason`, `userAgent`, and `responseStatus.code`
`event.source.component`, `event.requestURI`, and `event.verb`
`auditID`, `sourceIPs`, and `requestReceivedTimestamp`
questions.explanation: The audit log fields identifying actor and action are: `user.username` (who), `verb` (what — `delete`), `objectRef.namespace` (where — `prod`), `objectRef.resource` (type — `secrets`), and `objectRef.name` (which specific Secret). `event.source.component` is not a real audit log field. `auditID` is a correlation identifier. `annotations.authorization.k8s.io/reason` explains the authorization decision but doesn't identify the specific actor and target. `objectRef.resource`, and `objectRef.name`

questions.question: During incident response on a compromised microservice, the IR lead replaces the running pod with a freshly pulled image rather than execing in to clean up. The team's images are immutable — no in-place writes, no package manager, no shell. What is the key runtime-security advantage of immutability for incident response?
options: Pods can be recovered to a known-good state by simply replacing them with the original image — no risk of leftover attacker artefacts persisting in a writable filesystem, and no drift between the image and what is running
Immutability prevents the network policies attached to the pod from being modified by an attacker; otherwise NetworkPolicy objects could be edited from inside the pod
Immutable containers automatically expire and self-restart every 24 hours, so attackers can never maintain persistence beyond a single day
Immutability makes the kernel itself read-only, so even kernel-level rootkits cannot operate against a worker node hosting an immutable container
questions.explanation: The key advantage of `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` for incident response is signal clarity: normal application behavior cannot modify the filesystem, so any detected write or modification is definitively attacker activity. This eliminates false positives from legitimate app behavior. Traditional mutable containers make forensics harder because you can't distinguish attacker writes from normal application writes. Immutable containers don't have special pause/resume capabilities, don't automatically hash filesystems, and are not implemented at the CPU level.

questions.question: Forensic logs show attackers reading `/proc/1/environ` inside containers, extracting environment variables (including a database URL with embedded credentials) that were passed via the Pod spec's `env:` block. Which mitigation best addresses this exact class of leak?
options: Stop placing credentials in the Pod's `env:` block; mount them from Secrets as files (with restrictive permissions) or fetch them at runtime from a secrets manager — `/proc/1/environ` no longer carries them
Set `hostPID: true` on all pods so /proc namespaces are unified; this would broaden access rather than reduce credential exposure
Add a NetworkPolicy denying egress from the pod; this stops exfiltration of credentials but does not prevent the in-container read of /proc/1/environ
Switch the container runtime from containerd to CRI-O; both runtimes expose /proc/1/environ identically and the change has no effect on this leak
questions.explanation: The correct Falco condition uses `open_read` (macro for read-access file opens), `container` (container context macro), and `fd.name=/proc/1/environ` (full file path field). This fires when any container opens `/proc/1/environ` for reading. `syscall.arg.path` is not a valid Falco field. `file_access`, `namespace=container`, and `path.startswith` are not valid Falco syntax. `fd.directory` and `fd.filename` are not standard Falco fields — use `fd.name` for the full path.

questions.question: A runtime security incident is detected in a container. You need to capture its filesystem for forensic analysis without affecting other containers. What is the safest approach?
options: Use `crictl` on the node to locate the container's overlay filesystem layers and capture them directly from the host
Run `kubectl cp <pod>:/ /forensics/` to copy the entire container filesystem to an investigation host
Run `kubectl exec <pod> -- tar -czf /tmp/rootfs.tar.gz /` to archive the container's filesystem
Use `kubectl debug --copy-to` to create an exact copy of the Pod for forensic analysis
questions.explanation: Using `crictl` on the node to inspect and capture the overlay filesystem layers directly from the host is the safest forensic approach. It's non-intrusive — you don't run commands inside the potentially compromised container (avoiding running attacker tools or alerting the attacker). `kubectl exec` runs inside the compromised environment. `kubectl cp /` may miss filesystem metadata, symlinks, and overlay nuances. `kubectl debug --copy-to` creates a copy but the process of copying may modify the original state.

questions.question: Your audit policy logs Secrets at `RequestResponse` level, exposing base64 Secret values in logs. How do you log Secret access without capturing values?
options: Set `level: Request` for Secrets — captures write request bodies but not response bodies containing Secret data
Exclude Secrets entirely with `level: None` to prevent any Secret data from appearing in audit logs
Set `level: RequestResponse` with a redaction admission webhook to strip Secret data before logging
Set `level: Metadata` for Secrets — logs who accessed which Secret and when, without capturing the body
questions.explanation: `level: Metadata` logs the request metadata — user, timestamp, resource name, namespace, verb — without capturing any request or response body. This satisfies audit requirements (who accessed which Secret, when) without leaking the Secret value. `level: Request` logs the request body (write operations) but for reads, the Secret value is in the response. `level: None` leaves no audit trail. There is no built-in redaction mechanism in Kubernetes audit logging.

questions.question: You have a RuntimeClass `gvisor` with handler `runsc`. You want all Pods in the `untrusted` namespace to automatically use gVisor without modifying individual Pod specs. What enforces this automatically?
options: Add `runtimeClass: gvisor` as a namespace annotation to propagate it to all Pods at creation
Create a ValidatingWebhookConfiguration that rejects Pods in `untrusted` that don't have `runtimeClassName: gvisor`
Set `runtimeClassName: gvisor` in the namespace's LimitRange object to apply it to all Pods
Create a MutatingAdmissionWebhook (or OPA Gatekeeper/Kyverno mutation policy) that injects `spec.runtimeClassName: gvisor` into all Pods in the `untrusted` namespace
questions.explanation: The only way to automatically inject `runtimeClassName` into Pod specs is via a MutatingAdmissionWebhook — either a custom webhook or a policy engine with mutation support (OPA Gatekeeper MutationPolicy, Kyverno ClusterPolicy with `mutate`). LimitRange does not configure runtime classes. Namespace annotations are not propagated to Pod specs. A ValidatingWebhookConfiguration can enforce the requirement (reject pods lacking it) but cannot inject the value — injection requires mutation.

questions.question: A team wants to reduce the blast radius of a process running inside a container that gets RCE'd. Which TWO Pod-level settings most directly reduce that blast radius?
options: `securityContext.runAsNonRoot: true` — forces the workload to run as a non-root UID so capabilities and file ownership do not default to root inside the container
`securityContext.privileged: true` — grants the container near-host capabilities; the OPPOSITE of containment
`securityContext.capabilities.drop: ["ALL"]` — strips all Linux capabilities, leaving the process unable to perform privileged kernel operations even as root
`hostNetwork: true` — joins the container to the host's network namespace; broadens blast radius rather than reducing it
questions.explanation: Running as non-root prevents trivially exploitable root-only kernel paths. A read-only root filesystem stops attackers from writing webshells or persistent payloads. `privileged: true` GIVES the container near-host capabilities. `hostNetwork: true` shares the node's network namespace, exposing host services.
